title: The widow of Nain (Luke 7:11–17)
hook: he sees a widow burying her only son and says: don't weep

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Roman officer who said I am not worthy. Your line was only say the word. Did you send a kind word across a distance? Day five hundred twenty-seven.

Two crowds on one road. One is coming toward a small town called Nain: Jesus, his disciples, and a lot of people following, talking, maybe laughing, full of the news from Capernaum. The other crowd is coming out of the town gate. Slow. Quiet, except for the crying. A funeral. In front, men carry a body on an open bier. Behind them walks a woman. Luke tells us everything we need to know in one sentence: the dead man was "the only son of his mother, and she was a widow." She has already buried her husband. Now her only son. And the two crowds meet at the gate.
screen: `AN ONLY SON, AND SHE A WIDOW.`

segments.voice: Some readers point out that in that world a widow with no son could be left without income or protection. If so, this woman is burying her child and her future on the same day. Then Luke writes: "And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not." Notice: nobody asks him for anything. No one sends for him, no friends lower anyone through a roof. He sees her, and that's enough. The Greek word for compassion is splanchnizomai, related to a word for the inner organs; some readers translate it as being moved in the gut, a pull deep inside at someone else's pain. Then he does something unexpected at a funeral: "he came and touched the bier: and they that bare him stood still." The whole procession stops. "And he said, Young man, I say unto thee, Arise. And he that was dead sat up, and began to speak. And he delivered him to his mother." That last phrase, he delivered him to his mother, nearly repeats the words of 1 Kings about Elijah, when he raised a widow's son in Zarephath. The crowd at the gate says, "a great prophet is risen up among us," and, "God hath visited his people." This story begins not with a request or with faith, but with someone noticing a grieving stranger and being moved. Christian readers have seen God's own heart there: a God who sees the widow before anyone asks.
screen: then, large: `WHEN THE LORD SAW HER, HE HAD COMPASSION ON HER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice a stranger's grief. Settle, and breathe. Grief is often quiet. The man sitting too long in his parked car. The woman on the train staring at nothing. The voice on a phone call that sounds worn thin. Bring to mind a stranger you've seen lately who might have been carrying something. You don't know their story. You don't need to. Just let yourself be moved, the way Luke describes. Breathe in their heaviness; breathe out care toward them. Then imagine the smallest kindness you could offer a stranger like that today: holding a door, a patient answer, a real hello. If you pray, you can hold that stranger before God. If you don't, simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Splanchnizomai, Luke's Greek word for being moved with compassion, deep in the gut: a mother burying her only son meets Jesus at the gate, and before anyone asks, he is moved and gives her son back.
Your line: he had compassion on her. Today, look a little longer at the people you pass, and let one stranger's sadness move you to one small kindness. Day five hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Some churches read the widow of Nain at funerals and in times of grief, as a picture of Jesus noticing sorrow before anyone asks.

fork.reveal: nobody asks. Jesus sees her, is moved with compassion, touches the bier and raises the young man, and gives him back to his mother.

original.note: Greek: to be moved with compassion. related to splanchna, the inner organs.

trapdoor: what you thought: another miracle story.
what it means: Jesus notices a grieving widow, unasked, and is moved to give her son back, and with him her future.
what a scholar hears: "he delivered him to his mother" repeats the words of 1 Kings 17:23 about Elijah at Zarephath, and the crowd says: a great prophet.

notes: The widow's economic vulnerability is a standard historical reading. Confirm framing.
splanchnizomai from splanchna (inner organs): standard lexicon.
Echo of 1 Kings 17:23 ('delivered him unto his mother') is widely noted, and the Greek (Septuagint and Luke) match closely. Confirm 'almost word for word'.
